definition: The interdisciplinary field concerned with ensuring AI systems behave reliably, avoid unintended harmful behavior, and remain aligned with human values, especially as capabilities increase.
details: AI safety research spans technical work on alignment and robustness as well as broader questions about societal risks from increasingly capable AI systems, ranging from near-term harms to longer-term existential considerations.

explainer.lead: AI safety is the work of making AI systems behave reliably and avoid causing unintended harm, while keeping their behavior aligned with human values. It matters because reliability and value alignment become increasingly important as AI systems become more capable.

tiers.eli5: AI safety is like teaching a very capable helper not just to finish jobs, but to do them without causing accidents and to keep caring about what people actually want. As the helper becomes more capable, adults check more carefully that it behaves reliably. They also think about problems that could happen now and much bigger problems that could happen later.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply AI safety by examining alignment and robustness during development and deployment, then reassessing risks as capabilities or use settings change. The work can address immediate product harms as well as broader societal risks. A key pitfall is treating a successful test as proof of safety, or focusing only on long-term existential concerns while overlooking near-term harms.
tiers.paperLevel: AI safety can be expressed as an objective for a system S with capabilities C: as C increases, S should behave reliably, avoid unintended harmful behavior, and remain aligned with human values. The field combines technical research on alignment and robustness with analysis of near-term societal harms and longer-term existential risks. It is not a single formula or metric, and reliability, harm avoidance, and value alignment cannot be established by one test alone.

explainer.example: Before deploying an AI assistant, a team finds that some unexpected inputs lead to harmful responses. AI safety work would examine that robustness failure and whether the assistant’s behavior matches its intended human values, rather than judging it only on whether it completes requests.

usedIn.name: Alignment research
usedIn.detail: Studies how AI systems can remain aligned with human values as their capabilities increase.

usedIn.name: Robustness engineering
usedIn.detail: Examines whether AI systems behave reliably rather than producing unintended harmful behavior.

usedIn.name: AI deployment
usedIn.detail: Considers near-term harms and unintended behavior when increasingly capable systems are put into use.

usedIn.name: Societal risk assessment
usedIn.detail: Addresses broader risks from capable AI, including longer-term existential considerations.

explainer.intuition: Making an AI system good at a task is not enough: it should also behave reliably and avoid harmful ways of pursuing that task. AI safety adds the question of whether increasingly capable systems continue to act in accordance with human values.
howItWorks: Identify unintended harmful behavior and near-term societal risks.
Study technical alignment with human values.
Examine robustness and reliability as capabilities increase.
Consider longer-term risks, including existential considerations.
explainer.whyItMatters: Greater AI capability can make unreliable or misaligned behavior more consequential. AI safety connects immediate harms with longer-term societal and existential considerations instead of treating capability alone as sufficient.
misconceptions: AI safety is only about distant existential risk; it also includes near-term harms.
A system that performs its task well is not necessarily reliable or aligned with human values.
AI safety is not solely a technical subject; it is an interdisciplinary field.
